transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello Mr. Thompson, it is good to see you again today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Hello doctor. It is a bit chilly in here, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It can be. I wanted to sit down with you for a few minutes to talk about your recent chemotherapy cycle and some results we've seen.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, the medicine. I've been feeling quite poorly lately. Very tired. I suppose that's just what happens at my age.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand you've been feeling very worn out. However, I need to tell you that something went wrong with the dosing of your medication last time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We used your weight from several months ago to calculate the dose, instead of using your current weight. Because you have lost a lot of weight recently, you received a higher dose of chemotherapy than you should have.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Well, I have lost weight. The cancer does that. I'm sure I'm just feeling the effects of the illness.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it's common to lose weight with your condition, but this specific fatigue is because of a dosing error. I am sorry for any confusion this has caused.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't follow. Are you saying the medicine is too strong?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes. The dose was too high because the calculation was based on an old weight. We were very busy in the clinic that day and the current weight wasn't updated in the system.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's all very confusing. I just thought I was getting older. It's a natural thing, isn't it? To feel weak?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is natural to feel some fatigue, but this was an extra burden on your body that shouldn't have happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So you made a mistake?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, the team made an error in the calculation.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't know. It seems more likely that the cancer is just progressing. That's why I'm tired.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see why it feels that way, and it's frustrating when you're trying to make sense of why you feel so bad. But the blood tests show that the dose was indeed too high.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My hearing aid is acting up. Could you say that again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I said the blood tests show that the dose of medicine was too high because we used the wrong weight.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I see. But surely a little bit more medicine doesn't do much?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It can cause more toxicity, which is why you are feeling so exhausted.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I suppose. I just feel like you're worrying over nothing. I've had a lot of these treatments now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is certainly worrying to feel this way, but we need to be honest about what happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what now? Do I just keep taking it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, we are going to adjust your dose immediately. We will use your exact weight from this morning to make sure the next one is correct.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When does that happen?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The next infusion is scheduled for Tuesday. We will have the new dose ready by then.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Tuesday. I'll have to tell my daughter to drive me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That sounds like a good plan. I will also have the nurse check your blood counts on Monday just to be sure you've recovered from the last dose.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Monday and Tuesday. I can remember that.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll make sure the nurse writes that down for you on a slip of paper before you leave.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you, doctor. I still think I'm just old, but I'll trust you.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Thompson. We will keep a very close eye on you.

H.justification: The resident allows the patient to finish all turns, remains patient despite the patient's repeated denial of the error, and uses no rushing language.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the second turn using lay language, but there were no explicit checks for patient comprehension (e.g., 'Does that make sense?').

A.justification: While a direct apology was used, it was diluted by an excuse regarding being 'very busy in the clinic that day'.

R.justification: The resident named a specific emotion ('frustrating') and engaged with the patient's content regarding his fatigue and age.

T.justification: The resident provided specific next steps with timelines (Monday blood counts, Tuesday infusion) and a patient role (daughter driving), but did not address how to prevent the error in the future.
